newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs insist Moslem gunmen leave Bosnian village.
newsitem.headline: Serbs insist Moslem gunmen leave Bosnian village.

text.p: Bosnian Serb police have extended a deadline for Moslem gunmen to leave a ruined village in eastern Bosnia and have so far acted with restraint, NATO sources said.
Bosnian Serb interior minister Dragan Kijac earlier announced a 1500 GMT deadline on Monday for the men to clear out of the eastern village of Jusici, near a former front line.
A source in the NATO-led peace force (IFOR), who asked not to be named, said later that Kijac had postponed the deadline to Wednesday to allow time for negotiations.
"Kijac is being reasonable. We understand he's given another 48 hours before (Serb) police do anything," the source said.

IFOR spokesmen said the village was calm on Monday evening and the Serb police had not taken any action against the Moslem men of military-age who had entered the village saying they wanted to repair their ruined homes.
"We have assurances from the Serb republic police they will do nothing precipitous and keep us informed what they want to do," Major Simon Haselock said.
Over the weekend, Russian IFOR troops said they found submachineguns and more than 20 grenades on the men who moved into the village, which is almost completely destroyed.
IFOR commanders have voiced concern over groups carrying weapons into the "zone of separation", where all weapons are banned under the terms of the Dayton peace agreement.
The Moslems said 52 families had come to repair their homes and Bosnian state television denied the men had brought in guns and grenades.
Analysts said tensions in Jusici illustrated how communal authorities were still vying for territory since the signing of the Dayton accord last December.
They said Moslem authorities were pushing to reclaim Moslem villages near the former front line in the strategic Sapna area in eastern Bosnia.

By moving in armed men, some of whom were not former residents, the authorities were apparently interested in provoking a violent Serb response which would force IFOR troops to defend them, analysts said.
The Serb authorities were in turn obstructing any efforts to allow Moslems to return to their pre-war homes, particularly in disputed, strategic territory.
Major Brett Boudreau, another IFOR spokesman, told reporters the Dayton agreement ensures the right of war refugees to come back to their homes, but only under safe conditions.
Returning refugees to sensitive areas in the "zone of separation" required a patient, "phased approach" which should be coordinated with refugee agencies, he said.
Last month, a similar attempt by Moslems to enter the nearby village of Mahala led to a violent confrontation with Serb police. IFOR ultimately blamed both sides.
Fatija Ibrahimovic, 51, was one of 150 Moslems who have now moved back to Jusici, near Sapna, after living in Moslem- controlled Tuzla since the war started in 1992.
"I came back because I want to die in my house, now that I wasn't given a chance to live a decent life in it," Ibrahimovic said.
Serbs living in the nearby village of Malesici, one kilometre (mile) to the south, vowed to expel the Moslems if they tried to stay.
